orig_9709_p3_log_definitions_laws.description: Read logarithms as exponents, keep bases and arguments valid, and use the logarithm laws to rewrite expressions.

sections.title: What is a logarithm telling me?
sections.label: Read an exponent
sections.intro: \(\log_a u=t\) means \(a^t=u\). For a real logarithm, require \(u>0\), \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\). A negative answer is possible. It represents a reciprocal power of the base.

blocks.html: For a valid base, \(\log_a1=0\) and \(\log_a a=1\). In this course \(\log_{10}\) denotes the common logarithm and the calculator's log key gives base 10.

blocks.title: Recover both exponents
blocks.hint: Express the first argument as a power of \(10\). For the second, write \(16\) and \(8\) as powers of \(2\).

retry.feedback: A positive exponent of 10 gives a number greater than 1.
Write the target as a power of the stated base. The exponent of 2 in the target is 3.

sections.title: Which inputs and bases are allowed?
sections.label: Check the domain
sections.intro: Require every original argument to be strictly positive. With a variable base, also require a positive base different from \(1\). Keep these conditions through every rearrangement.

blocks.title: Keep both strict boundaries
blocks.hint: Write one strict inequality for each argument, then intersect them.
blocks.solution: The first argument needs \(x>\frac32\) and the second needs \(x<9\). The domain is \(\frac32<x<9\).

retry.feedback: Both boundary values make an original argument zero.
The second logarithm supplies an upper bound.

blocks.title: Spot a forbidden variable base
blocks.prompt: For which of these values of \(x\) is \(\log_{x-2}9\) defined?
blocks.hint: The base must be positive and different from \(1\).
blocks.solution: \(x=4\) gives base \(2\). The other values give base \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\).

retry.feedback: A base of one cannot generate an inverse exponential.

sections.title: How do I combine logarithms?
sections.label: Use the logarithm laws
sections.intro: For a fixed valid base \(a\) and positive arguments \(u,v\), addition of logarithms corresponds to multiplication of arguments. Subtraction corresponds to division.

blocks.html: \(\log_a u+\log_a v=\log_a(uv)\), \(\log_a u-\log_a v=\log_a\!\left(\frac uv\right)\) and \(k\log_a u=\log_a(u^k)\).
\(\log_a(u+v)\) requires the sum to be evaluated as a single argument. The sum law applies to \(\log_a u+\log_a v\) and produces a product inside the logarithm.

blocks.title: Choose the right order of operations
blocks.hint: Deal with the coefficient first. Multiply by the last argument and divide by the squared argument.

glossary.definition: The positive number \(a\ne1\) raised to a power in \(a^t\).

examples.title: Read negative and fractional exponents
examples.question: Find \(\log_{10}(0.0001)\) and \(\log_9 3\) exactly.
solution: Write \(0.0001=10^{-4}\). The exponent of base \(10\) is \(-4\).
Write \(3=9^{\frac12}\). The exponent of base \(9\) is \(\frac12\).

examples.title: Intersect two argument conditions
examples.question: Find the real domain of \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_3(7-x)\).
solution: The first logarithm requires \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\).
The second requires \(7-x>0\), so \(x<7\). Together the conditions give \(1<x<7\).

examples.title: Use a coefficient and a quotient
examples.question: Evaluate \(\log_3 108-2\log_3 2-\log_3 3\) exactly.
solution: Move the coefficient inside as a power to get \(2\log_3 2=\log_3(2^2)\).
Combine the two subtractions to obtain \(\log_3\!\left(\frac{108}{4\cdot3}\right)=\log_3 9=2\).

revision.body:
Read the exponent

\(\log_a u=t\) if and only if \(a^t=u\), where \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\) and \(u>0\). In particular \(\log_a1=0\) and \(\log_a a=1\).

Keep the original domain

Apply the positivity test to every argument. For \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_3(7-x)\), the answer is \(1<x<7\).

Use one base

\(\log_a u+\log_a v=\log_a(uv)\). Use \(\log_a\!\left(\frac uv\right)\) for subtraction and \(\log_a(u^k)\) for \(k\log_a u\).

Read exact powers

\(\log_{10}(0.0001)=-4\) and \(\log_9 3=\frac12\). A fractional exponent can be read as a root.
revision.checks:
• Check that the base is positive and different from one.
  • Check the original arguments before combining.
  • Move a coefficient inside as a power.
revision.examTip: Write a line that shows the combined argument. This makes the products, quotients and powers easy to check.

orig_9709_p3_log_logarithmic_equations.description: Apply the log laws to equations, record the original domain and check every candidate solution.

sections.title: How do I remove a single logarithm?
sections.label: Undo one logarithm
sections.intro: Isolate the logarithm. The equation \(\log_a u=k\) fixes its argument at \(u=a^k\). Solve for the unknown inside the argument and check the original condition \(u>0\).

blocks.title: Use a reciprocal base
blocks.hint: Rewrite the equation as \(3x-2=\left(\frac12\right)^{-2}\).

sections.title: Why can a product give an invalid root?
sections.label: Combine a sum
sections.intro: Set the domain from the separate logarithms. After combining the arguments you may obtain a polynomial with more solutions than the original equation.

blocks.html: A product of two negative numbers is positive. The original individual arguments must still be positive.

blocks.title: Submit only the roots that survive
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\log_3(x-4)+\log_3(x+4)=2\). Give the complete real solution set.
blocks.hint: Require \(x>4\) before rewriting the left side as one logarithm.

sections.title: How do I clear a logarithmic quotient?
sections.label: Combine a difference
sections.intro: Subtracting two logarithms of the same base produces the logarithm of a quotient. Keep the condition that its denominator is positive before multiplying.

blocks.title: Recover the exact root
blocks.hint: The combined argument is \(\frac{5x+1}{2x-1}\). Set it equal to \(2^2\).

sections.title: What if the equation is quadratic in a logarithm?
sections.label: Use a substitution
sections.intro: When you see \((\log_a x)^2\) and \(\log_a x\), let \(t=\log_a x\). Solve the quadratic in \(t\) first. Each real value of \(t\) gives one positive value \(x=a^t\).

blocks.title: Return both roots in x
blocks.hint: First solve \((t-2)(t+1)=0\) for \(t=\log_2 x\). Then undo the substitution.
blocks.solution: \(t=2\) gives \(x=4\) and \(t=-1\) gives \(x=\frac12\). Both values are positive.

retry.feedback: Those are values of \(t\). Convert them back using \(x=2^t\).
The root \(t=-1\) is valid too. A negative logarithm has a positive argument below one.

glossary.definition: The values allowed by every expression in the given equation.
A value obtained during working that still needs checking in the original equation.
A temporary variable that exposes a simpler equation.

examples.title: Isolate and exponentiate
examples.question: Solve \(\log_3(2x-5)=2\).
solution: The argument condition is \(2x-5>0\), so \(x>\frac52\).
\(2x-5=3^2=9\), giving \(x=7\). Here the argument is \(9\), which satisfies the original equation.

examples.title: Solve a quadratic and check the domain
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2(x-2)+\log_2(x+1)=2\).
solution: Both arguments are positive only for \(x>2\).
Factor as \((x-3)(x+2)=0\). Keep \(x=3\). At \(x=-2\) both original arguments are negative.

examples.title: Turn a log difference into a linear equation
examples.question: Solve \(\log_5(2x-1)-\log_5(x-3)=1\).
solution: The conditions \(2x-1>0\) and \(x-3>0\) reduce to \(x>3\).
The combined argument satisfies \(\frac{2x-1}{x-3}=5\). Multiplication gives \(2x-1=5x-15\).
Therefore \(x=\frac{14}{3}\), which is in the original domain.

examples.title: Return from the substituted variable
examples.question: Solve \((\log_3 x)^2-3\log_3 x+2=0\).
solution: Use \(x=3^t\) at both values. The roots are \(3\) and \(9\).

revision.body:
Write the domain first

Each original argument must be positive. A later combined logarithm can hide an invalid branch.

Use one logarithm

\(\log_a u=k\) gives \(u=a^k\). Combine sums as products and differences as quotients before undoing the logarithm.

Check polynomial candidates

\(\log_2(x-2)+\log_2(x+1)=2\) gives \(x^2-x-6=0\). Candidates are \(3\) and \(-2\). The domain \(x>2\) leaves \(x=3\).

Undo a substitution

If \(t=\log_a x\), a quadratic in \(t\) can give two values. Convert every value using \(x=a^t\).
revision.checks:
• Keep the domain beside your working.
  • Clear a denominator only on the allowed domain.
  • List all real roots that pass the original check.
revision.examTip: When a candidate is rejected, state the exact argument or original domain condition that it violates.

orig_9709_p3_log_exponential_equations.description: Solve equations and inequalities with an unknown exponent using matching bases, logarithms and positive substitutions.

sections.title: Can I use a common base?
sections.label: Match the bases
sections.intro: If both sides can be written as powers of one positive base different from \(1\), equal outputs have equal exponents. Rewrite the bases before expanding the products in the exponents.

blocks.title: Equate complete exponents
blocks.hint: Use base 3 on both sides. Apply the exponent multiplier to the whole bracket.

sections.title: When should I take logarithms?
sections.label: Take logs on both sides
sections.intro: First isolate the exponential. For \(a^{g(x)}=c>0\), take the same logarithm on both sides and use \(g(x)\ln a=\ln c\). Keep full calculator precision until the final line.

blocks.title: Give the rounded value of the exponent
blocks.hint: After division by \(5\), take the natural logarithm of both sides.

fields.label: Value of x to three decimal places

sections.title: How can a quadratic appear in an exponential?
sections.label: Use a positive substitution
sections.intro: If a term is the square of another exponential, use \(t=a^x\) and keep \(t>0\). Convert only positive roots back to the original variable.

blocks.title: Reject an impossible exponential value
blocks.hint: Use \(t=3^x\) to factor the quadratic, and keep only values of \(t\) that are possible.

retry.feedback: These are roots of the quadratic in \(t\). Reject the negative value and convert back to \(x\).

sections.title: When does an inequality reverse?
sections.label: Use the direction of change
sections.intro: For \(a>1\), comparing values of \(a^x\) keeps the same order of exponents. For \(0<a<1\) it reverses. In logarithmic working this reversal occurs when you divide by \(\ln a<0\).

blocks.title: Find the correct ray and endpoint
blocks.hint: Write \(8\) as \(\left(\frac12\right)^{-3}\). Think about the order of the exponents.
blocks.solution: The base is below one, so \(3x+1\le-3\). The answer is \(x\le-\frac43\), including equality.

retry.feedback: For a decreasing exponential, the order of the exponents is reversed.

glossary.definition: For \(a>1\), larger exponents give larger values of \(a^x\).
For \(0<a<1\), larger exponents give smaller values of \(a^x\).

examples.title: Keep the exact answer until the final line
examples.question: Solve \(4\cdot3^{2x-1}=17\). Give the answer to three decimal places.
solution: Divide by \(4\). This gives a positive right-hand side \(\frac{17}{4}\).
Taking natural logarithms gives \((2x-1)\ln 3=\ln\!\left(\frac{17}{4}\right)\).
Hence \(x=\frac{1+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{17}{4}\right)}{\ln 3}}{2}\approx1.159\).

examples.title: Solve for a positive exponential
examples.question: Solve \(4^x-5\cdot2^x+4=0\).
solution: Let \(t=2^x>0\). Since \(4^x=t^2\), the equation becomes \((t-1)(t-4)=0\).
Both roots are positive. \(2^x=1\) gives \(x=0\), and \(2^x=4\) gives \(x=2\).

examples.title: Compare powers of a base below one
examples.question: Solve \(\left(\frac13\right)^{2x-1}<\frac1{27}\).
solution: The right side equals \(\left(\frac13\right)^3\). A larger exponent gives a smaller value.
Therefore \(2x-1>3\) and \(x>2\). The inequality is strict, so exclude \(2\).

revision.body:
Match the bases

\(a^{g(x)}=a^{h(x)}\) gives \(g(x)=h(x)\) when \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\). Rewrite each base and multiply the whole exponent.

Take logarithms

With \(a^{g(x)}=c>0\), use \(g(x)\ln a=\ln c\). Solve exactly first and round only the final value.

Use a positive substitution

Let \(t=a^x>0\) when both \(a^{2x}\) and \(a^x\) occur. Solve in \(t\), then recover \(x\) for each positive root.

Choose the inequality direction

\(a^x\) increases for \(a>1\) and decreases for \(0<a<1\). For example \(\left(\frac13\right)^{2x-1}<\left(\frac13\right)^3\) gives \(2x-1>3\), so \(x>2\).
revision.checks:
• Check the base and the sign of any logarithm you divide by.
  • Keep equality at any included boundary.
  • Reject non-positive values of a substituted exponential.
revision.examTip: If no common base is available, an exact logarithmic expression is a good intermediate line even when a decimal is requested.

orig_9709_p3_log_natural_logs.description: Connect the natural exponential and logarithm as inverse functions, then use their domains and ordering to solve problems.

sections.title: What makes natural logarithms special?
sections.label: Read the inverse graphs
sections.intro: \(e\) is a fixed positive constant greater than \(1\) with approximate value \(2.718\). The natural logarithm is the inverse of \(y=e^x\). Every real exponent gives one positive output.

blocks.html: \(\ln(e^x)=x\) for all real \(x\). Also \(e^{\ln x}=x\) for \(x>0\). Swapping input and output reflects the graph in \(y=x\).

figure.alt: A blue exponential curve crosses the y-axis at (0, 1). A green logarithmic curve crosses the x-axis at (1, 0). They are mirror images across the dashed diagonal y = x.
figure.caption: \(y=e^x\) has horizontal asymptote \(y=0\). Its inverse \(y=\ln x\) has vertical asymptote \(x=0\).

blocks.title: Connect an intercept and an asymptote
blocks.hint: Reflect the corresponding features of the natural exponential graph in the line \(y=x\).
blocks.solution: \(\ln 1=0\) and the vertical asymptote is \(x=0\). The graph is defined to the right of the vertical axis.

sections.title: What does the sign of k change?
sections.label: Sketch growth and decay
sections.intro: All curves \(y=e^{kx}\) pass through \((0,1)\). For \(k>0\), the graph rises to the right and approaches \(y=0\) at the left. For \(k<0\), the graph falls to the right and approaches \(y=0\) at the right. When \(k=0\), the graph is the horizontal line \(y=1\).

blocks.html: The sketch shows one increasing and one decreasing exponential. Identify the same intercept and the direction of each curve.

figure.alt: The blue curve y equals e to the x rises to the right. The green curve y equals e to the minus two x falls to the right. Both pass through (0, 1) and approach the x-axis at opposite ends.
figure.caption: A negative exponent multiplier reverses the direction of change. Neither curve meets the horizontal asymptote \(y=0\).

blocks.title: Compare growth and decay at a point
blocks.hint: Evaluate the exponents at \(x=-1\) before comparing the outputs.

sections.title: When may I cancel an exponential and a log?
sections.label: Undo inverse operations
sections.intro: Apply the inverse relationship to the whole exponent or argument. In \(e^{\ln u}\), check \(u>0\) before replacing the expression with \(u\).

blocks.title: Check an inverse pair and a domain
blocks.hint: Undo the two inverse functions. The second logarithm still requires \(3x+2>0\).

blocks.title: Isolate the exponent
blocks.hint: Take \(\ln\) of both sides, then solve a linear equation for \(x\).

fields.label: Value of x to three decimal places

sections.title: How does the domain affect an inequality?
sections.label: Solve on the original domain
sections.intro: \(\ln x\) increases on its positive domain. Compare its arguments after recording their positivity. If you then divide by a negative coefficient of \(x\), reverse the inequality at that step.

blocks.html: Equality is allowed at \(x=1\) in this example. The boundary \(x=-\frac32\) is still excluded because the argument is zero there.

blocks.title: Show both strict bounds
blocks.hint: First require \(9-3x>0\). Then convert the logarithmic comparison to a linear inequality and intersect the two conditions.
blocks.solution: The domain gives \(x<3\). The comparison \(9-3x<6\) gives \(x>1\). The solution is \(1<x<3\).

retry.feedback: The comparison supplies the lower bound. The original logarithm also supplies an upper bound.
Both boundaries are strict. One gives equality and the other gives an undefined logarithm.

glossary.definition: \(\ln x\) is the logarithm to base \(e\), defined for \(x>0\).
Applying one function and then its inverse recovers the original allowed input.
A line that a curve approaches. Here an axis is approached without being reached.

examples.title: Compare domains, ranges and axis crossings
examples.question: State the domain, range and axis intercept of \(e^x\) and of \(\ln x\).
solution: For \(e^x\), any real \(x\) is allowed. The range is \(y>0\). Its \(y\)-intercept is \((0,1)\).
For \(\ln x\), only \(x>0\) is allowed. The range is all real \(y\). Its \(x\)-intercept is \((1,0)\).

examples.title: Use the exponent to predict the shape
examples.question: Describe the shape of \(y=e^{-2x}\) and evaluate it at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\).
solution: As \(x\) increases, \(-2x\) decreases. Because \(e^t\) increases with \(t\), the curve is decreasing.
The curve goes through \((0,1)\). At \(x=1\) the output is \(e^{-2}\), which lies between \(0\) and \(1\). It therefore approaches \(0\) on the right without reaching it.

examples.title: Solve two inverse equations
examples.question: Solve \(\ln(e^{3x-1})=8\) and then solve \(e^{\ln(2x-4)}=8\).
solution: In the first equation the exponential already has positive output. Use \(\ln(e^{3x-1})=3x-1\) to get \(x=3\).
In the second equation require \(2x-4>0\). On that domain \(e^{\ln(2x-4)}=2x-4\), so \(x=6\) is allowed.

examples.title: Solve a natural logarithmic equation
examples.question: Solve \(2\ln(x-1)=\ln9\).
solution: The logarithm requires \(x>1\). Divide both sides by \(2\) to get \(\ln(x-1)=\ln3\).
Equal natural logarithms have equal positive arguments, so \(x-1=3\) and \(x=4\). This lies in the original domain.

examples.title: Keep both domain and comparison
examples.question: Solve \(\ln(2x+3)\le\ln5\).
solution: Require \(2x+3>0\), so \(x>-\frac32\).
Since the logarithm is increasing, \(2x+3\le5\), so \(x\le1\). Combining the restrictions gives \(-\frac32<x\le1\).

revision.body:
Match inverse inputs and outputs

\(\ln(e^x)=x\) for all real \(x\). \(e^{\ln x}=x\) requires \(x>0\). The inverse graphs reflect in \(y=x\).

Locate asymptotes and intercepts

\(e^x\) has intercept \((0,1)\) and horizontal asymptote \(y=0\). \(\ln x\) has intercept \((1,0)\) and vertical asymptote \(x=0\).

Use the sign of k

\(e^{kx}\) grows for \(k>0\) and decays for \(k<0\). All these curves pass through \((0,1)\) and have positive outputs.

Keep the domain in comparisons

Because \(\ln x\) increases, \(\ln(2x+3)\le\ln5\) gives \(2x+3\le5\). Combine with \(2x+3>0\) to get \(-\frac32<x\le1\).
revision.checks:
• Apply the inverse operation to the entire expression.
  • Retain every original positivity condition.
  • Reverse an inequality when dividing by a negative number.
revision.examTip: At a boundary where an argument is zero, the logarithm is undefined. That boundary is excluded even when the comparison includes equality.

orig_9709_p3_log_linearisation.description: Choose transformed axes, read a straight line, and recover constants in power and exponential models.

sections.title: Which axes straighten a power model?
sections.label: Choose log–log axes
sections.intro: For \(y=Ax^n\) with \(A>0\) and \(x>0\), take natural logarithms to get \(\ln y=n\ln x+\ln A\). Plot \(\ln y\) vertically against \(\ln x\) horizontally. The gradient is \(n\) and the vertical intercept is \(\ln A\).

blocks.title: Use the transformed points
blocks.prompt: The straight line with coordinates \((\ln x,\ln y)\) passes through \((0,\ln7)\) and \((\ln2,\ln56)\). Find \(A\) and \(n\) in \(y=Ax^n\).
blocks.hint: The first point gives \(\ln A\). The change in height is \(\ln\!\left(\frac{56}{7}\right)\).
blocks.solution: \(\ln A=\ln7\) gives \(A=7\). The gradient is \(\frac{\ln8}{\ln2}=3\), so \(n=3\).

sections.title: Which axes straighten an exponential model?
sections.label: Choose semi-log axes
sections.intro: For \(y=Ab^x\) with \(A,b>0\), use \(\ln y=(\ln b)x+\ln A\). Here \(x\) remains unchanged. If \(y=Ae^{kx}\), the slope is \(k\) and the intercept is \(\ln A\). For the same model, \(b=e^k\).

blocks.title: Undo the log on the gradient
blocks.prompt: For \(y=Ab^x\), a graph of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) gives \(\ln y=\ln8+x\ln\!\left(\frac32\right)\). Find \(A\) and \(b\).
blocks.hint: The vertical intercept and gradient are \(\ln A\) and \(\ln b\) respectively.
blocks.solution: The intercept gives \(A=8\) and the gradient gives \(b=\frac32\).

retry.feedback: The gradient is positive, so the original exponential base must be greater than one.

sections.title: How do I find an intercept from two points?
sections.label: Use the line equation
sections.intro: Find the gradient using transformed coordinates. Substitute one of those points into \(\ln y=mx+c\) to find the intercept \(c\). Convert using \(A=e^c\).

blocks.html: The points \((2,5)\) and \((6,1)\) below are in coordinates \((x,\ln y)\). Use them directly to calculate the line.

figure.alt: Horizontal x-axis and vertical ln y-axis with points (2, 5) and (6, 1). The line descends with gradient minus one. Extending it to x equals zero gives a vertical intercept of seven.
figure.caption: The vertical coordinate is \(\ln y\). The intercept \(7\) means \(\ln A=7\) in an exponential model, so \(A=e^7\).

blocks.title: Use both transformed coordinates
blocks.prompt: The line of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) passes through \((2,6)\) and \((5,12)\). Find \(k\) and \(\ln A\) in the model \(y=Ae^{kx}\).
blocks.hint: Compute the gradient first. Substitute either point into \(\ln y=kx+\ln A\).

sections.title: How do I choose between two possible models?
sections.label: Compare transformed scales
sections.intro: Compare at least three points. With exact data, a candidate requires a consistent straight line on its chosen axes. With measured data, look for an approximately straight pattern. Two points by themselves always lie on a straight line.

blocks.title: Identify the model and both constants
blocks.prompt: At \(x=1,2,3\), the outputs are \(48,24,12\). Choose the model that fits all three values exactly. Give its multiplier \(A\) and its base or exponent, as appropriate.
blocks.hint: The \(x\)-steps are equal. Compare successive output ratios and check which transformed axes give a constant gradient.
blocks.solution: Each increase of one in \(x\) halves \(y\), so \(y=A\left(\frac12\right)^x\). Using \((1,48)\) gives \(A=96\).

fields.label: Value of the base or exponent

glossary.definition: Choosing new coordinates so a model gives a straight-line graph.
Change in the vertical coordinate divided by change in the horizontal coordinate.
Vertical coordinate of the line at zero on the selected horizontal scale.

examples.title: Read the gradient and recover the multiplier
examples.question: The straight line of \(\ln y\) against \(\ln x\) for \(y=Ax^n\) goes through \((0,\ln5)\) and \((\ln2,\ln20)\). Find \(A\) and \(n\).
solution: The first point is at horizontal coordinate \(0\). It gives \(\ln A=\ln5\), so \(A=5\).
The gradient is \(\frac{\ln20-\ln5}{\ln2}=\frac{\ln4}{\ln2}=2\). Thus \(y=5x^2\).

examples.title: Recover the exponential base
examples.question: For \(y=Ab^x\), a graph of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) gives \(\ln y=\ln12-x\ln3\). Find \(A\) and \(b\).
solution: The vertical intercept is \(\ln12\), so \(A=12\).
The gradient is \(-\ln3=\ln\!\left(\frac13\right)\), hence \(b=\frac13\). This is a decay model.

examples.title: Find the intercept even when no point lies on the axis
examples.question: A line of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) passes through \((2,5)\) and \((6,1)\). Find \(k\) and \(A\) for \(y=Ae^{kx}\).
solution: The gradient is \(\frac{1-5}{6-2}=-1\), so \(k=-1\).
Put \((2,5)\) into \(\ln y=-x+c\), obtaining \(5=-2+c\). Hence \(c=7\) and \(A=e^7\).

examples.title: Recognise a power pattern
examples.question: At \(x=1,2,4\) the outputs are \(5,20,80\) respectively. Choose between a power model \(y=Ax^n\) and an exponential model \(y=Ab^x\) and find its constants.
solution: Doubling \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(4\) in both steps. On log–log axes, each horizontal step is \(\ln2\) and each vertical step is \(\ln4\). Thus \(n=2\).
The point \((1,5)\) in original coordinates gives \(A=5\). The relation \(y=5x^2\) fits all three points.
On semi-log axes the vertical changes are both \(\ln4\), but the horizontal changes are \(1\) and \(2\). The slopes on those axes differ.

revision.body:
Power model

\(y=Ax^n\) gives \(\ln y=n\ln x+\ln A\) for \(x>0\) and \(A>0\). Plot \(\ln y\) against \(\ln x\). Gradient \(n\), intercept \(\ln A\).

Exponential model

\(y=Ab^x\) gives \(\ln y=(\ln b)x+\ln A\). Plot \(\ln y\) against \(x\). Gradient \(\ln b\), intercept \(\ln A\). For \(y=Ae^{kx}\) the gradient is \(k\).

Recover the original constants

Find \(m\) and \(c\) using the coordinates on the chosen axes. Use \(A=e^c\). In \(y=Ab^x\) use \(b=e^m\). In \(y=Ax^n\) use \(n=m\).

Use both transformed points

In a semi-log plot, \((2,5)\) and \((6,1)\) give gradient \(-1\) and intercept \(7\). This gives \(y=e^7e^{-x}\). Compare at least three data points when choosing a model.
revision.checks:
• Read the labels on both transformed axes.
  • Use a substituted point to calculate the intercept.
  • Check the reconstructed model in the original coordinates.
revision.examTip: State the full equation in \(x\) and \(y\) when both constants are found. Use the actual axes to justify the model type.
